cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: Film movements are coherent groups of filmmakers who share aesthetic principles, production methods and ideological commitments during a specific historical period.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: Italian Neo-Realism emerged after World War II, rejecting studio artificiality in favour of location shooting, non-professional actors and stories about working-class struggle.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: The French New Wave of the late 1950s and 1960s challenged mainstream French cinema with location filming, handheld camera, jump cuts and self-reflexive storytelling.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: German Expressionism of the 1920s used distorted set design, exaggerated shadows and stylised performance to convey psychological turmoil and social anxiety in post-World War I Germany.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: Soviet Montage of the 1920s, led by Eisenstein and Vertov, used dynamic editing techniques to create meaning through the collision of images rather than continuous narrative.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: Italian Neo-Realist films such as Bicycle Thieves and Rome, Open City depicted poverty, unemployment and moral crisis with documentary-like authenticity and compassion.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: French New Wave directors including Godard and Truffaut were originally critics at Cahiers du Cinema who championed auteur theory before becoming filmmakers themselves.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: German Expressionist films such as The Cabinet of Dr Caligari and Nosferatu used oblique angles, distorted perspectives and chiaroscuro lighting to externalise inner states.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: Later movements include British Social Realism, Czech New Wave, Brazilian Cinema Novo and Dogme 95, each responding to specific cultural and political circumstances.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: Film movements often arise during periods of social upheaval, when existing cinematic conventions seem inadequate to represent changed realities.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: The influence of early film movements persists in contemporary cinema: Neo-Realism in social realist filmmaking, Expressionism in horror and film noir, the New Wave in indie cinema.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Film Movements
cards.back: Understanding film movements helps contextualise individual films within broader artistic, political and historical frameworks rather than treating them as isolated works.
